title: A Cellar for the Visitor
premise: Yara Nystrom, a skeptical property surveyor, arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for a silent estate and finds a home that measures him back: mirrors lag one second behind reality, floorboards remember footsteps, and a cellar door hums an old harvest song whose final verse no one will sing. As the house's previous 'visitors' surface in its reflections—people who stayed too long and were kept—Yara realizes his appraisal report is actually a contract of belonging, and that the estate's heirs intend to deliver him as payment. To survive the rising of the harvest moon, he must learn the song's last verse from the trapped visitors without singing along, using it to unbind the house. In the end Yara frees the kept ones by giving the house what it truly wanted—not a resident, but a witness—and walks out at dawn with a report no one will ever file.
about_author: Felix Almeida is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties across the northern coast, where he collected more stories than measurements. He writes horror about houses that refuse to be empty, and claims he has never slept in one twice.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Yara Nystrom accepts an unusually generous appraisal job for Hollowmere House from an estate firm with no listed principals. His POV establishes his creed: everything has a price, nothing is haunted, only unmaintained. The emotional beat is dry professional confidence, undercut slightly by the client's insistence he stay overnight to 'complete the survey.'

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: Yara measures the house room by room, but his laser rangefinder returns different numbers on every pass, always larger when he isn't looking directly at a wall. POV stays tight on Yara; the beat is unease rationalized away as equipment error. He notes a locked cellar door humming faintly, like a throat clearing.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: That evening Yara catches his reflection in a hallway mirror raising its hand after he does. Testing every mirror in the house, he confirms each reflects exactly one second behind. His POV; the beat shifts from skepticism to controlled denial—he documents the anomaly as 'electrical interference' and refuses to leave before finishing the job.

chapters.title: The Previous Appraiser
chapters.summary: In an upstairs study Yara finds a 1974 appraisal report, unfinished, signed by a surveyor named Edvard Lune—the same handwriting as the commission letter. The mirror shows someone standing behind him who isn't there. Beat: dread arriving through paperwork, the horror of bureaucracy turned uncanny.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Sings
chapters.summary: The cellar door's hum resolves into melody—a harvest song, verses one through three, then silence where a fourth should be. When Yara hums along involuntarily, the house settles around him like a dog lying down. His POV; the beat is the first seduction: the house likes him, and being liked feels dangerously like belonging.

chapters.title: The Heirs Arrive
chapters.summary: Three representatives of the estate arrive at dusk—polite, identical smiles, names that don't match their signatures. They explain the appraisal must be 'witnessed' overnight for validity. Yara's POV; the beat is social menace, the horror of hospitality, as they set a place for him at dinner he never agreed to attend.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Kept
chapters.summary: At dinner, the mirrors show extra guests seated among them—faded figures watching hungrily. One whispers to Yara through the glass: 'Don't sign the last page.' The heirs talk about harvest traditions. Beat: loyalty vs. truth begins to fracture the scene; Yara realizes politeness is the trap's mechanism.

chapters.title: Edvard's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Alone at night, Yara deciphers Edvard Lune's marginalia: the song's fourth verse is a binding, and whoever sings it aloud becomes part of the house's count. The mirrors now show Yara's reflection remaining in rooms after he leaves. Beat: the price of survival becomes explicit—stay invisible or be inventoried.

chapters.title: Rooms That Count
chapters.summary: Yara tries to leave; the front door opens onto the kitchen. Every exit routes back inside. He maps the house obsessively, discovering it gains a room each time he stops believing he can go. His POV frays between panic and methodical note-taking. Beat: claustrophobia as cartography.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Pantry Mirror
chapters.summary: A kept visitor—Maren, missing since 1961—speaks to Yara through a pantry mirror, teaching him the song's first three verses properly and warning that the heirs collect witnesses who sing. Beat: the first genuine alliance; Yara's skepticism bends into belief not of ghosts, but of people.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Living
chapters.summary: The heirs present Yara with his own appraisal report, nearly complete, needing only his signature on the final page—which reads 'occupant: one.' He stalls, claiming professional standards require a full structural inspection of the cellar. Beat: negotiation as survival; Yara weaponizes his own professionalism.

chapters.title: Below the Floorboards
chapters.summary: The heirs unlock the cellar. Inside: no monsters, only rows of labeled shelves holding belongings of every kept visitor, and a stone basin where the song originates. Yara hears the fourth verse clearly for the first time and barely clamps his mouth shut. Beat: awe curdling into terror; the house's heart is a hunger for participation.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren reveals the truth: she stayed willingly once, trading her voice for her sister's release. The kept can't teach the fourth verse—they can only show it. She offers to guide Yara if he promises to speak their names outside, making them witnessed. Beat: loyalty vs. truth crystallizes; keeping his promise may cost him his escape.

chapters.title: The Heirs' Patience Ends
chapters.summary: With the harvest moon two nights away, the heirs stop pretending. They move Yara's belongings into the master bedroom, hang his coat by the door, and begin introducing him to neighbors who see only the house. Beat: identity erosion; the horror of being pre-remembered.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Yara spends the day memorizing the fourth verse silently, mouthing it while Maren and the other kept shape the words in mirrors. Each rehearsal, the house grows warmer toward him—lights brighten, doors open unbidden. Beat: the terrible intimacy of being wanted; belonging offered as anesthesia.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: A neighbor visits, chats warmly with Yara about decades of shared history he doesn't have. In the mirror, the neighbor is empty clothes. Yara understands: the house manufactures belonging wholesale. Beat: grief—for everyone who ever accepted a comfort too good to question.

chapters.title: Moonrise Terms
chapters.summary: The heirs offer final terms: sign, sing, and want for nothing forever—or refuse and be taken anyway at moonrise. Yara asks for one hour to 'finish the report.' Alone, he drafts two endings: one signature, one witness statement naming every kept visitor. Beat: resolve hardening into sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Moonlight floods the house; the mirrors stop lagging and start leading. The heirs escort Yara to the cellar basin, where the song swells to the edge of the fourth verse. Maren mouths 'remember us.' Beat: climax threshold—everything narrows to breath and choice.

chapters.title: The Verse Unbound
chapters.summary: At the basin, Yara speaks the fourth verse instead of singing it—naming it, dissecting it, reading it aloud as evidence rather than joining it. The binding inverts: the song requires willing voices, and testimony is not consent. The house convulses; the shelves topple; the kept step out of every mirror. Beat: catharsis through the very skepticism that endangered him.

chapters.title: Witnesses
chapters.summary: Yara stands on the lawn under the waning moon and reads the names of all forty-one kept visitors aloud until dawn, each name releasing a figure into the grey light. Maren leaves last, pressing Edvard Lune's unfinished report into his hands. Beat: mourning and release intertwined; loyalty honored over truth's cold efficiency.

chapters.title: Appraisal: Final
chapters.summary: Hollowmere House stands empty and ordinary, its mirrors exactly one second honest. Yara files a report declaring the property structurally unsound and unfit for occupancy—technically true, since it no longer holds anyone. The estate firm dissolves. Beat: quiet triumph; the bureaucratic gesture as exorcism.

chapters.title: The Song He Didn't Sing
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Yara hears four bars of the harvest song from a stranger's open window and walks the other way, humming something of his own choosing. In his pocket, Maren's sister's address waits for a visit he promised. Beat: earned peace with a scar—the knowledge that belonging, freely chosen, is the only kind worth having.
